phil:singer: Peter Singer is an Australian moral philosopher, born in 1946, who is among the most influential proponents of contemporary utilitarianism. His 1975 book Animal Liberation helped launch the modern animal-rights movement by arguing that the interests of sentient beings deserve equal moral consideration regardless of species. He is also known for demanding accounts of our obligations to the global poor and for helping to shape the effective altruism movement, which seeks to do the most good with available resources.
phil:kierkegaard: Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was a Danish philosopher and theologian widely regarded as a forerunner of existentialism. Writing often under elaborate pseudonyms, he emphasized the concrete situation of the individual, the priority of subjective and passionate commitment over abstract systems, and the anxiety and despair that accompany human freedom. His works, including Either/Or and Fear and Trembling, explore stages of life and the notion of a personal, risk-laden "leap" of faith.
phil:husserl: Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) was a German-speaking philosopher and mathematician who founded phenomenology, the systematic study of the structures of consciousness as they are experienced from the first-person point of view. He argued that inquiry should return "to the things themselves" by bracketing assumptions about the external world and describing how objects are given to awareness, a method he called the epoché. His work, especially Logical Investigations and Ideas, profoundly shaped later thinkers such as Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty.
phil:heidegger: Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) was a German philosopher whose work reoriented phenomenology toward the question of the meaning of being. In his major work Being and Time, he analyzed human existence, which he called Dasein, in terms of its being-in-the-world, its temporality, and its confrontation with mortality and anxiety. Enormously influential on existentialism and hermeneutics, his legacy remains controversial because of his membership in and support for the Nazi Party.
phil:sartre: Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) was a French philosopher, novelist, and playwright who became the public face of twentieth-century existentialism. In Being and Nothingness he argued that human beings have no fixed essence and are "condemned to be free," making themselves through their choices and bearing full responsibility for them, with self-deception described as "bad faith." A committed public intellectual, he later drew existentialism toward Marxism and declined the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964.
phil:beauvoir: Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a French philosopher and writer whose work joined existentialist ethics with a pioneering analysis of women's situation. Her landmark study The Second Sex argued that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman," treating femininity as a socially constructed condition of subordination rather than a natural given, and it became a foundational text for modern feminist thought. She also developed an existentialist account of freedom and moral responsibility in The Ethics of Ambiguity.
phil:camus: Albert Camus (1913–1960) was a French-Algerian writer and thinker associated with existentialism, though he preferred to call his outlook a philosophy of the absurd. He held that human beings crave meaning in a universe that offers none, and in The Myth of Sisyphus he argued that one should confront this absurdity without either suicide or false hope, embracing life in defiance. His novels, including The Stranger and The Plague, dramatize these themes, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.
phil:merleau-ponty: Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1908–1961) was a French phenomenologist best known for placing the lived, perceiving body at the center of philosophy. In his major work Phenomenology of Perception he argued that we do not primarily encounter the world as detached minds but through embodied, situated perception, challenging sharp divisions between mind and body and between subject and object. His thought influenced later work in philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and the study of embodiment.
phil:frankl: Viktor Frankl (1905–1997) was an Austrian psychiatrist and thinker whose experiences surviving Nazi concentration camps informed a philosophy centered on the human search for meaning. In his widely read book Man's Search for Meaning, he argued that even in the most extreme suffering people retain the freedom to choose their attitude and to find purpose. He founded logotherapy, a form of existential psychotherapy holding that the will to meaning is a primary human drive.
phil:levinas: Emmanuel Levinas (1906–1995) was a French philosopher of Lithuanian Jewish origin who made ethics, rather than metaphysics or epistemology, the foundation of philosophy. Drawing on phenomenology and Jewish thought, he argued in works such as Totality and Infinity that the encounter with the face of the Other imposes an infinite responsibility that precedes and grounds all knowledge and freedom. His emphasis on responsibility for the other person deeply influenced later ethical and continental philosophy.
phil:turing: Alan Turing (1912–1954) was a British mathematician and logician whose work laid the theoretical foundations of computing and shaped philosophical debate about the mind. He formalized the notion of computation with the abstract "Turing machine" and, in his 1950 essay Computing Machinery and Intelligence, proposed what became known as the Turing test as a practical criterion for machine intelligence. His contributions, including his codebreaking work in the Second World War, made him a central figure in the philosophy of mind and artificial intelligence.
phil:searle: John Searle, born in 1932, is an American philosopher known for his work in the philosophy of mind and language. He is famous for the Chinese Room argument, which contends that a system manipulating symbols by rules can produce apparently intelligent responses without any genuine understanding, challenging strong claims about artificial intelligence. He also developed influential theories of speech acts and of intentionality, the mind's capacity to be directed at objects and states of affairs.
phil:putnam: Hilary Putnam (1926–2016) was an American philosopher whose wide-ranging work shaped the philosophy of mind, language, and science. He proposed functionalism, the view that mental states are defined by their causal roles rather than their physical makeup, and later criticized it, and his Twin Earth thought experiment argued that the meanings of words depend partly on the external world, so "meanings just ain't in the head." Known for repeatedly revising his own positions, he moved from metaphysical realism toward a more pragmatist "internal realism."
phil:chalmers: David Chalmers, born in 1966, is an Australian philosopher recognized for sharpening contemporary debates about consciousness. He coined the phrase the "hard problem of consciousness" to distinguish the puzzle of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience from the easier problems of explaining cognitive functions. His book The Conscious Mind defends the view that consciousness cannot be fully reduced to the physical, and he has also written influentially on the mind's extension into its environment and on the philosophy of virtual reality.
phil:dennett: Daniel Dennett (1942–2024) was an American philosopher and cognitive scientist known for a thoroughly naturalistic account of the mind. He argued that consciousness is not a unified inner theater but the product of many parallel processes, a view developed in Consciousness Explained, and he treated beliefs and desires as useful predictive constructs adopted from what he called the intentional stance. A prominent defender of Darwinian thinking and a leading figure in the New Atheism, he sought to explain mind, meaning, and even religion within a scientific worldview.
